utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. Good morning. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-97-24-A, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Registrar. We'd like to make sure that the interpreters are in place. They are. I see the appellant, Mr. Stakic, is in the courtroom. Mr. Stakic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, I can hear and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stakic. You may sit down. Defence and the Prosecution, I take it that you can hear me. Could I ask for the appearances of the parties, first for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is senior appeals counsel Mark McKeon. At the table with me here is our case manager, Mr. Andres Vatter, and at the table behind me are senior appeals counsel Helen Brady and appeals counsel Barbara Goy and Xavier Tracol. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McKeon. Could we now please have appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and John Ostojic for Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. I would like to explain how we are going to proceed through this hearing. As the registrar announced, we are hearing today the case of the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic. Mr. Stakic was indicted for genocide and complicity in genocide, murder, extermination, persecutions, inhumane acts and deportations as crimes against humanity, and murder as a war crime. According to the indictment, the appellant committed these crimes between about 30th of April, 1992 and 30th of September, 1992, in the municipality of Prijedor. On 31 July 2003, Trial Chamber II of this Tribunal issued a judgement in Mr. Stakic's case, finding him not guilty of the crime of genocide, Count 1; complicity in genocide, Count 2; and forcible transfer as a crime against humanity, Count 8. The Trial Chamber found the appellant guilty of extermination as a crime against humanity, Count 4; murder, as a violation of the laws and customs of war, Count 5; and persecutions, as a crime against humanity, Count 6; incorporating the crimes of murder as a crime against humanity, Count 3; and deportation as a crime against humanity, Count 7. The appellant was sentenced to life imprisonment. Mr. Stakic and the Prosecution have each appealed different aspects of the trial judgement. The hearings before the Appeals Chamber this week serve two purposes. First, we will hear new testimony from Witness BT106, and second, we will hear oral argument on the merits of the appeals in this case. This morning we will begin by hearing from Witness BT106. After this testimony, we'll take a 30-minute break, and then reconvene to hear the Prosecution's submissions on the merits of its appeal. We will adjourn for the day after hearing the Prosecution's submissions. All day tomorrow and on Thursday morning, we will continue hearing argument on the merits of the appeals. Before we hear Witness BT106's testimony, I want to recall why this witness has been asked to appear before the Appeals Chamber today. On 25 January 2005, the Appeals Chamber granted, in part, a Defence motion seeking, inter alia, to have certain statements by Witness BT106 admitted into evidence pursuant to Rule 115. These statements, given in an out-of-court interview with a representative of the OTP in 2003, concern Mr. Stakic and other people in the Prijedor municipality relevant to this case. After the Defence made clear that it did not intend to call Witness BT106 to give oral testimony, the Appeals Chamber, acting proprio motu, rendered a decision summoning BT106 to testify at this hearing. In its decision, the Appeals Chamber explained that hearing Witness BT106 may help it to assess the reliability of the admitted statements, which concern core issues of this case. Witness BT106 is then appearing as a witness for the Appeals Chamber. As the Appeals Chamber explained in the Scheduling Order it issued on 26 September 2005, the examination of Witness BT106 will proceed as follows: The Bench will examine Witness BT106 for approximately 15 minutes, maybe more than that. After the Bench concludes its questioning, the parties will have the chance, if they wish, to conduct cross-examination. The Prosecution will be allowed to cross-examine the witness first and it will have a maximum of 30 minutes in which to do so. After that, I will give the floor to the Defence. The Defence will likewise be allotted 30 minutes in which to pose questions. I wish to remind the parties that they need not use all the time allocated. After the parties have finished cross-examining Witness BT106, the Bench may pose additional questions. Witness BT106's counsel will be present during the testimony. Pursuant to Rule 75(F), this Tribunal has in the past employed two protective measures, pseudonyms and closed sessions, when hearing testimony for Witness BT106. The Appeals Chamber has decided that these measures should remain in place. As we are about to begin the examination of Witness BT106, I ask that the registrar kindly close our session now. We go into a closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Please be seated. We shall now start the hearing on the merits of the appeals. Before we begin, let me briefly recall the grounds of appeal raised by the parties. The first, second, and third grounds of appeal by the Prosecution concern genocide, a crime of which Mr. Stakic was acquitted. In its first ground of appeal, the Prosecution argues that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that Mr. Stakic did not have the requisite intent for genocide. In its second ground of appeal, the Prosecution argues that, in determining that Mr. Stakic had not committed acts specified in Article 4 of the Statute, was genocidal intent, the Trial Chamber improperly failed to consider conditions at certain camps set up by the authorities in Prijedor, conditions under which deportations and expulsions were carried out and measured that deprived Bosnian and Croats of work and housing in Prijedor. In its third ground of appeal, the Prosecution argues that the Trial Chamber should have defined the group victimised by the alleged genocide as "non-Serbs" and that in any event, the Trial Chamber should have found that Bosnian Croats, like Bosnian Muslims, were targeted for crimes in Prijedor because of their ethnicity. The Prosecution's fourth ground of appeal relates to cumulative convictions. The Prosecution argues that the Trial Chamber erred in law by failing to enter independent convictions against the appellant for persecutions, murder, and deportations as crimes against humanity, and instead only entering a conviction for persecutions as a crime against humanity. I turn now to the Defence's grounds of appeal. The first relates to the alleged expulsion of the indictment. The Defence argues here, inter alia, that the Trial Chamber erred by relying on acts that Mr. Stakic allegedly took before or after the period specified in the indictment. In its second ground of appeal, the Defence argue that the Trial Chamber committed numerous errors of law and fact and thus denied Mr. Stakic a fair trial. Specifically, the Defence challenges the Trial Chamber's refusal to admit expert evidence on various topics. The Trial Chamber's denial of Mr. Stakic's motion for a mistrial based on the Prosecution's breach of its Rule 68 disclosure obligations; the Trial Chamber's refusal to let the Defence introduce certain written statements pursuant to Rule 92 bis; the Trial Chamber's decision to admit certain written statements offered by the Prosecution; the Trial Chamber's decision not to warn certain Defence witnesses about the obligation to tell the truth; and the Trial Chamber's admission of certain evidence the Defence deems untrustworthy. In its third ground of appeal, the Defence submits that the Trial Chamber drew impermissible circumstances from circumstantial evidence regarding Mr. Stakic's state of mind and the extent to which he knew about the crimes being committed and thereby caused a miscarriage of justice. In its fourth ground of appeal, the Defence contends that the Trial Chamber erred in law and in fact in its application of various elements of Article 5 of the Statute; in particular, the Defence challenges both the Trial Chamber's finding that there was a widespread and systematic attack on civilian populations in Prijedor municipality and its findings that Mr. Stakic committed the offences of extermination, persecutions, and deportation. The Defence's fifth ground of appeal relates to Article 3 of the Statute. The Defence argues that the Trial Chamber erred in finding a nexus between Mr. Stakic's acts and the armed conflict, a requirement for Article 3, liability. The Trial Chamber erred in convicting him of murder under Article 3 of the Statute. In its sixth ground of appeal, the Defence argues that the Trial Chamber erred in imposing a life sentence. In its seventh ground of appeal, the Defence argues that the Trial Chamber erred in convicting Mr. Stakic for both persecutions and exterminations as crimes against humanity. According to the Defence, Mr. Stakic's conviction for the crime of extermination is impermissibly cumulative with his conviction for the crime of persecutions. Now I would like to remind the parties that an appeal is not a trial de novo. The Appeals Chamber will consider alleged errors of law which would invalidate the judgement, and in exceptional circumstances it will consider other questions of law of importance to the Tribunal's jurisprudence. The Tribunal will only consider alleged errors of fact that would result in a miscarriage of justice. As the parties should be well aware, the Appeals Chamber considers questions of law de novo, but requires an appellant who alleges errors of fact to demonstrate that no reasonable trier of fact could have reached the conclusion being challenged. Parties should be as clear and precise as possible in the presentation of their arguments. Before giving the floor to the Prosecution, I would remind the parties that in an order issued on 26 September 2005, the Appeals Chamber invited the parties to, inter alia, further develop their submissions on a number of specific issues. The Appeals Chamber does wish to hear argument on these issues, but this should not prevent the parties from raising other issues they wish to touch on in this hearing. I will now give the floor to the Prosecution, which has one hour and 30 minutes to present its submissions. The Prosecution. Mr. McKeon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: You may start.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. I will be presenting this morning the Prosecution's arguments on the first, the second, and the third grounds of appeal dealing with genocide. My colleague, Mr. Xavier Tracol, will present the Prosecution's arguments on the fourth ground of appeal, dealing with cumulative convictions. And I would like to ask to reserve 15 minutes of our time at the end for Mr. Tracol to present the argument on the fourth ground. Before I begin, I would like to let the Chamber know how I will be structuring my argument this morning. I will start with the third ground of appeal. Our basic argument there is that the Trial Chamber, by defining the target group of genocide too narrowly, did not consider all the evidence it should have in determining whether Dr. Stakic had genocidal intent. The Trial Chamber should have concluded that the target group was non-Serbs. Through a legal error, however, the Trial Chamber concluded it could not define the target group by a negative criterion. I will then turn to our first and second ground of appeal, and our argument there is based on the factual findings of the judgement. We argue that given these factual findings, no reasonable trier of fact could have concluded that Dr. Stakic did not have genocidal intent. As we address the first ground of appeal, we will attempt to answer the question of what caused the Trial Chamber to evaluate the evidence improperly in this case, and we will show that the answer may be found, at least in part, in three legal errors we submit were committed by the Trial Chamber in evaluating the evidence. First, the Trial Chamber confused motive with intent. Second, the judgement reflects the Trial Chamber's view that genocide could only be accomplished by killing all Muslims or, as we now argue, all non-Serbs, and this error demonstrates a lack of understanding that a group can be destroyed and genocide can occur in ways other than by killing all the members of the targeted group. And finally, we will argue that the Trial Chamber erred in evaluating the evidence under Article 4(2)(c), deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part. And I would note that this last error corresponds to our second ground of appeal, which I will discuss at the end of the submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Counsel, would you be so kind, when you refer to specific matters, please relate that to paragraphs in the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd now like to turn to the third ground of appeal, defining the target group. On September 9th, 2004, in an historical statement before the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. US Senate Foreign Relations Committee, US Secretary of State Colin Powell described the ongoing events in the Darfur region of Sudan as "genocide." According to Secretary Powell, the target group of this genocide was non-Arab individuals and villagers. In the context of the Sudan, where it has been reported that there are more than 500 ethnic groups, this is the only designation that made sense of the facts on the ground. Your Honours, 12 years before Secretary Powell's declaration about the Sudan, a UN Commission of Experts, looking at the situation in Bosnia, reached a similar conclusion. In their final report, the Commission of Experts concluded that, if there are several or more than one victim group and each group, as such, is protected, it may be within the spirit and purpose of the convention to consider all the victim groups as a larger entity. The commission described a situation where an A group has defined a pluralistic, non-A group using national, ethnical, racial, or religious criterion for the definition. The Commission concluded that it could be relevant to analyse the fate of the non-A group along similar lines as if the non-A group had been homogenous. Given the fact that the Commission of Experts focussed much of their investigation on what happened in Prijedor, it should come as no surprise that the example they give matches the facts in this case so well. The approach suggested by the Commission of Experts has been accepted into the jurisprudence of this Tribunal in the Jelisic case. In that case, the Trial Chamber concluded that a group could be stigmatised by way of positive or negative criteria. A positive approach distinguishes a group by the characteristics which they deem to be particular to a national, ethnical, racial, or religious group. A negative approach consists of identifying individuals as not being part of the group to which the perpetrators of the crime consider that they themselves belong and which, to them, display specific national, ethnical, racial, or religious characteristics. All individuals thus rejected would, by exclusion, make up a distinct group. The Jelisic Trial Chamber agreed that it was consonant with the object and the purpose of the genocide convention to consider that its provisions also protect groups defined by exclusion where they have been stigmatised by the perpetrators in that way. In the view of the Jelisic Trial Chamber, thus, you correctly define a target group from the perspective, the subjective perspective, of the perpetrator, and it will depend on the facts of the case. Now, keeping in mind the caveat expressed by the Commission of Experts that the separate victim groups so combined must, as such, each already be protected by the genocide convention, we submit that this approach makes sense of the evidentiary burden placed on the Prosecution. The Prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the perpetrator had the specific intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial, or religious group as such. To determine the specific intent of the perpetrator, however, you must first identify what it is he is attempting to destroy, what he is trying to destroy. This means that the focus must be on the subjective view of the perpetrator. Let's say, for example, that the perpetrator is a member of a group A and he is trying to destroy a group B because of specific characteristics of group B and group C because of different specific characteristics of group C. On the facts of this case, it could make sense to analyse the acts against group B and C as if they were separate intended genocides. But what if the perpetrator is only going against groups B and C because neither one is group A, to which he belongs? In that case, from the point of view of the perpetrator, there are not two attempted genocides but only one. And in the latter case, the perpetrator himself has defined the target group by negative criterion. When analysing the perpetrator's intent, we submit, the trier of fact should analyse the intent he actually has and not some artificial construct based on a division of the targeted groups, which doesn't reflect the way the perpetrator allegedly viewed the situation. In the present case, the Trial Chamber erred because it concluded that it could not legally do that. Now, the approach accepted in the Jelisic Trial Chamber is consistent with other cases from this Tribunal and the Rwanda Tribunal that have defined the targeted group from the subjective perspective of the perpetrator. Citing Jelisic, for example, the Krstic Trial Chamber defined the relevant group by using as a criterion the stigmatisation of the group, notably by the perpetrators of the crime, on the basis of its perceived national, ethnical, racial, or religious characteristics. In Rutaganda, from Rwanda, the Trial Chamber found that membership of a group is, in essence, a subjective rather than an objective concept. The victim is perceived by the perpetrator of the genocide as belonging to a group slated for destruction. The Rutaganda case had followed a subjective approach used by the Trial Chambers in Kayishema, and this was later followed by the Trial Chamber in Bagilishema, which concluded that the perpetrators of genocide may characterise the target groups in ways that do not fully correspond to conceptions of the group shared generally or even by other segments of society. In such a case, the Chamber was of the opinion that on the evidence, if a victim was perceived by a perpetrator as belonging to a protected group, the victim could be considered by the Chamber as a member of the protected group for the purposes of genocide. Now let's come to what happened in the present case. The Trial Chamber in this case concluded that when more than one group is targeted, it is not appropriate to define the group in general terms as non-Serbs, thus rejecting the negative approach adopted in Jelisic and the subjective approach adopted in most of the remaining cases from the ICTR and ICTY. In so doing, the Trial Chamber ignored its own findings that the target of Dr. Stakic's genocidal acts was actually non-Serbs. I have several pages of examples that I'm not going to go through all of them, but I would like to highlight a few of the ones that I think are more telling. First of all, the word "non-Serb" or "non-Serbs" appears in the judgement 121 times. The crime-base section of the judgement - that's section 1E - is entitled "Acts committed against non-Serbs in the municipality of Prijedor." In paragraph 154 of the judgement, the attack on Hambarine and the Kozarac areas were deemed attempts to cleanse these areas of their non-Serb population. In paragraph 282, the systematic destruction of the town of Prijedor formed "part of the general attack against the non-Serb population." In paragraph 401, dealing with the camps, the Trial Chamber was satisfied that Dr. Stakic was aware that non-Serbs were detained in the camps on a discriminatory basis and that foreseeable crimes were being committed against them in the camps. Later, in paragraph 598, the Trial Chamber said that Dr. Stakic simply accepted that non-Serbs would and did die in the camp. The killings committed in the municipality during 1992 were deemed part of a campaign of annihilation of non-Serbs carried out by Serb police and military forces. That's paragraph 655. In paragraph 661, killings were perpetrated on a massive scale against the non-Serb population of Prijedor. The campaign of annihilation directed against the non-Serb population again is referred to. And finally, in reference to persecution, which has, as you know, a specific intent requirement, the target of Dr. Stakic's discriminatory intent was described as non-Serbs. In paragraph 819, the Court said there was a persecutorial campaign based on the intent to discriminate against all those who were non-Serb or who did not share the above-mentioned plan to consolidate Serbian control and dominance in the municipality of Prijedor. The Trial Chamber's approach was not based on any legal requirement and was inconsistent with the facts proven at trial, and it should be reversed. Before moving on to grounds 1 and 2, I'd like to deal here with two questions that were posed in advance of this hearing by the Chamber. The first is question number 4 that asks that we address the legal basis for defining a group protected under Article 4 as non-Serbs. I would just like to add this to what I've already said on that subject. I think there are two ways where the definition of the group is important under the genocide convention and under the Statute. First, we must be sure that the victim group is one that enjoys the protection of the genocide convention. For example, this must not be a case where the victim group is a political construct which is generally accepted as being beyond the reach of the protection of the genocide convention, which does not protect political groups. And second, we must analyse the specific intent of an accused to determine whether he had the intent to eliminate a protected group as such. So first is ensuring that there are protections given to the people that are targeted, and secondly, ensuring that we examine the intent of the accused. And I think I've already demonstrated how in this case defining the group in a negative fashion as non-Serbs is the best way to analyse the evidence of Dr. Stakic's intent in this case. So turning to the first issue, this is not a case where the Prosecution is seeking to expand the protection of the genocide convention beyond groups defined as a national, ethnical, racial, or religious group. Specifically, we are not here today urging that the protections be extended to any stable and permanent group, as was done in the Akayesu case, for example. I think there is no doubt that Bosnian Muslims, or at least no dispute in this case, that Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats were each separately protected groups under the genocide convention. Thus, every person defined as members of the larger group, non-Serb, is also a member of the smaller, protected group defined by ethnicity. The groups are merely being combined to analyse the intent of the accused. Thus, I submit, this meets the concerns expressed by the Commission of Experts that the groups combined in this fashion must, as such, be protected. Moreover, we would refer to the language of the convention which defines the protections as extending to groups defined by ethnicity, nationality, religion, or race. In a broader group, in a broader sense, an ethnic group is any group defined by ethnicity. If you have a group of people, say everyone in this room, from which you exclude everyone who is of one nationality, the remainder, by definition, is a group defined by ethnicity, the ethnicity they don't have. The genocide convention protects ethnic groups, not homogenous ethnic groups. The second question I'd like to address here is number 3, that we clarify the legal basis for adopting policy considerations in interpreting Article 4 of the Statute. I believe this question was provoked by paragraph 4.9 of the Prosecution's Appeal Brief, which stated that the approach espoused by the Trial Chamber was not supported by any authority, does not accord with the plain interpretation of Article 4, and is not based on any policy considerations. It is our position in this appeal that policy considerations Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. cannot be relied upon as an independent source of legal authority. However, policy considerations can be used as an aid in interpreting the Statute, particularly when, as here, the statutory language has been lifted directly from an international treaty, the 1948 Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide. The legal basis for using policy considerations in interpreting Article 4 is Articles 31 and 32 of the Vienna Convention on Treaties. The Appeal Chamber for the ICTR recognised in an interlocutory appeal in the Bagosora case that Article 31 of the Vienna Convention applied to the Statute of the ICTR. That's the decision of 8th of June, 1998, paragraphs 28 and 29. Here at the ICTY, Judges McDonald and Vohrah for the Tribunal recognised the application of the rules of treaty interpretation in the Vienna Convention in the Tadic jurisdictional appeal, paragraph 18. And I think that you will see from an analysis of that decision that what I'm going to say was used as a way to analyse the intent. Under Article 31 of the Vienna Convention, terms in a treaty are interpreted in context and in light of the treaty's object and purpose. The reference to the treaty's context and its object and purpose points towards a teleological or purposive standard of interpretation, which means, in our view, considering the mischief the treaty was designed to remedy. In that context, what we meant by policy considerations in 4.9 of our brief is that the Statute must be interpreted by considering which interpretation would be most effective in getting at the mischief criminalised by the genocide convention. At the same time, the Trial Chamber should have avoided an interpretation that doesn't reflect how the perpetrators of genocide actually view their targeted groups. And just to give a couple of examples from the Tribunal where this approach was followed, I think you can see it twice in the Tadic jurisdictional appeal, first in paragraph 166, dealing with Article 2 of the Statute. The Appeals Chamber looked to the object and purpose approach to determine the concept of protected persons within the context of ethnic conflicts. Elsewhere in the same judgement, paragraph 285, the Appeals Chamber against used the object and purpose standard to defend a comparably broad view of Article 5 of the Statute. So I think that by looking at the object and purpose, you are, in effect, calling upon the policy considerations that caused the treaty, or ultimately the Statute, to be enacted in the first place. I'd now like to turn to our first ground of appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I would like to check that my distinguished colleagues would not like to ask questions on this problem of non-Serb. I see I did provoke Judge Shahabuddeen to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. McKeon, do forgive me in case I have missed it. You have, I know, referred to a number of decisions on this question, and I was wondering whether those references included any contribution that the Appeals Chamber, whether of the ICTY or the ICTR, ever pronounced on this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: I believe that this answer is a question of first impression for the Appeals Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May I ask another question? You have argued most attractively, and I shall in due course, with the benefit of my colleagues' thinking, try to evaluate the arguments of both sides as I hear them. Tell me this: If you look at Article 4, paragraph 2, the second line, you see the words "as such." Do those words introduce any kind of nuance suggestive of the view that the reference to a national, ethnical, racial, or religious group has to be a reference to a particular group, not negatively defined?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would not myself interpret that language that way. I think from the previous cases, and I'm sorry that I can't give you chapter and verse of those cases at the moment, but that language has been interpreted as being placed into the convention to make sure that the target is the group and not the individuals in the group. And I think that's what it's trying to distinguish, that you are not targeting people of a certain race because you want to target them individually but because you want to target the group. And I think that language leaves open the question of how it is you define the group. I don't think it speaks to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I'm indebted to you, Mr. McKeon. I will consider it in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Other questions on that? No. Could I take you up on that for moment? You did make the argument that before turning to the aggregate term "non-Serbs," you look at the components in terms of qualifications and definition and in terms of intent to satisfy the requirements of the convention. And only after that specific assessment you go to the aggregate non-Serbs. Now, if you have to look at the specific component to satisfy yourself that in fact they meet the definitions contained in the convention on genocide and Article 4 of the Statute, what exactly is the legal purpose of the aggregate term "non-Serbs" and how does the use of that term meet the requirements of the convention regarding specific intent of arrest against a specific target group?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Just as an example, Your Honour, what you are trying to do is you are trying to focus on the intent of the perpetrator. And one of the things that you have to prove, that we have to prove, rather, and you have to be satisfied, a court as the trier of fact, is that the perpetrator intended to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnical, racial, or religious group. So we would submit that, when you're looking at the intent of the perpetrator, it may make sense to look at the victim groups the way the perpetrator looked at them, as a single, unified group. To determine, for example, whether a substantial part of that group has been targeted, you would look at the aggregate group the way the perpetrator looked at it. When you looked at, for example, whether the group was targeted to be destroyed in part, rather than breaking it up into component parts and trying to look at each individual group individually, which is not, as we would submit on the evidence, the way the perpetrator looked at it in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: In terms, coming back to Judge Shahabuddeen, my distinguished colleague Judge Shahabuddeen's point, this is a novel argument really in terms of the Appeals Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: It's a new argument before the Appeals Bench, but it's not a new argument before the Tribunals. It has, as we've cited in our brief, been considered and accepted in previous cases. It was rejected in this case, and I believe it was also rejected in the later case of Brdjanin, which followed this case, by the Trial Chamber, but otherwise the subjective approach has been used in the other cases in the Tribunal, both Tribunals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Have you seen anything in discussions pertaining to the genocide during the Second World War which would have formed some kind of a foundation for this aggregate term?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Nothing that I can cite from World War II, other than -- well, there's a couple of points that I can make, nothing that I can cite to. But first of all, I think that when we talk about World War II and the genocide, it was often talked about the Nazis as attempting to form an Aryan society and targeting non-Aryans by definition. Secondly, I think that from the point of view of targeting the Jews, the Nazis in World War II had defined ways of saying who was in the targeted group and who was not. Extensive definitions of who met the targeted group of being a Jew. Those may or may not have corresponded to how the persons themselves may have viewed themselves. They may have been targeted by the Nazis as a Jew, not viewed themselves that way, or vice versa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Fair enough. But those targeting definitions would be dealing with, say, Jews or Gypsies. I am interested in your point regarding the non-Aryan. I'm not aware of any sort of legal or genocidal type of lessons that we can draw from, but I'm perhaps not an expert on that and I would be happy to be guided by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Well, I'm certainly also not an expert on that, Your Honour. I would note that the genocide convention, of course, as you know came after World War II, and I think that the discussions, as I understand them, in defining the groups tended to focus on not so much this very question we've got here, do you define the group big or small, but had to do with things like political groups, whether political groups would be -- or linguistic groups would be protected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: And finally, what is the forensic advantage that you derive from the aggregate term that you would not derive from looking at the various components, Serbs, Croats, or Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: I think that what it does is it gives the Chamber an opportunity to look at the evidence as a whole. In this case, the Trial Chamber, for example, had trouble finding that there was a genocide against the Croats because of the small number of individuals that were involved relative to the size of the Bosnian Muslims. If they were combined, however, as they should have been, with the Bosnian Muslims as a targeted group, that wouldn't have been a problem, and the Trial Chamber could have considered in one group all the evidence of genocide, whether it was against a Bosnian Muslim or a Bosnian Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So the convention -- let me understand, that the convention speaks either of a group or a substantial part; right? That's how we dealt with it in Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: So say that you deal with Croats, you say, well, Croats do not reach that threshold of substantiality in terms of numbers, so you now aggregate them to the other group and say, Well, we have a larger group now, and therefore we can use the term "genocide" with regard to the mix?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Because I think it's within both the language and the object and purpose of the Statute to be able to do that. I mean, if we had a situation, let's say, where we had hundreds of small groups and you were targeting anyone who wasn't like you in a village, and that would consist of hundreds of nationalities, none of whom perhaps could raise to a level that, on an individual basis, would be protected, even though they're a group defined by ethnicity and the ethnicity of the people, but as a large construct and as a group, they are nevertheless targeted and they could in fact be destroyed completely and not in part. But if you don't allow the negative definition that group may never be within the reach of the genocide convention, even though it is a group that is defined by -- or could be defined by ethnicity, race, nationality, or religion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And as Judge Shahabuddeen said, we will give a very careful consideration to your arguments. Please proceed. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll now turn to the first ground of appeal. In the first ground of appeal, we allege that the Trial Chamber erred by failing to reach the correct conclusion that Dr. Stakic had the mens rea for genocide. There's a few preliminary points I'd like to make before getting into the argument. First, we are basing our appeal solely on the facts as found by the Trial Chamber. We are not asking this Appeals Chamber to re-evaluate the evidence to determine if those factual findings are correct. In his response to our appeal, Dr. Stakic has attempted to re-litigate many of those individual factual findings by citing evidence that he asserts brings those factual findings into doubt. To the extent he wants to do this, this is more properly done in his own appeal challenging the factual findings. The only question in our appeal is taking the facts as found by the Trial Chamber, could a reasonable trier of fact have concluded that Dr. Stakic did not have the mens rea for genocide? We submit the answer is no. There is only one reasonable conclusion, and it is not the one the Trial Chamber reached. Second, to the extent that legal errors were committed in evaluating this evidence, either by accepting our third ground of appeal, which we've already discussed, or the legal errors we will discuss later this morning in our first and second grounds of appeal, under the Blaskic case, the Appeals Chamber should apply the correct legal standard to the evidence contained in the trial record and then to determine whether it is itself convinced beyond a reasonable doubt as to the findings of guilt or innocence. At that point, if an incorrect legal standard was applied and this Chamber then applies the correct standard, there is no longer deference to the Trial Chamber's findings, and you must decide yourself the guilt or innocence. Although the Blaskic decision was framed in terms of appeals by the Defence against findings of guilt, there is no logical reason that we can see why a different standard should apply to Prosecution appeals against findings of innocence. My finally preliminary point is concerning joint criminal enterprise, and we will address later in this hearing, either tomorrow or Thursday morning, the specific questions that the Chamber had about joint criminal enterprise. I just want to touch on one point that relates to the genocide. In our opening brief, we asserted that the Trial Chamber should have found Dr. Stakic liable for committing genocide as a co-perpetrator or indirect co-perpetrator, but we argued alternatively that Dr. Stakic should also have been found liable as a participant in a joint criminal enterprise for genocide. We submitted that the focus should be on establishing the mens rea of Stakic and that of the other co-perpetrators at the horizontal level of the municipality of Prijedor. Now, to the extent that this Appeals Chamber accepts our submission that the factual conclusions of the Trial Chamber support only one reasonable conclusion, that is, that Dr. Stakic had the intent to destroy a national, ethnic, or religious group, we submit that same evidence demonstrates this intent was shared by all members of the horizontal JCE, particularly the members of the Prijedor Crisis Staff. Thus, the factual conclusions in paragraph 555 of the judgement that no one else on a horizontal level in the municipality of Prijedor had the dolus specialis for genocide was an error. We would also note that we are basing our appeal on the genocide at least solely on joint criminal enterprise 1, and as we stated in our reply brief that we filed in this matter, we are not basing it on any theory of joint criminal enterprise 3, even though I think subsequent developments since we filed our brief in the Brdjanin interlocutory appeal would support it. We are not relying on that. The principal argument that we make in our appeal is that if one considers only the factual findings made by the Trial Chamber, a reasonable trier of fact could only have concluded that Dr. Stakic had genocidal intent. In trying to discern genocidal intent, we are trying to parse out whether an attack on a particular group member is really directed at the larger group rather than that member as an individual. Victims must be selected because of their group membership and because of an intent directed at the group. Now, as has often been recognised, intent is a mental factor which is difficult to determine, and in the absence of a confession from the accused, his intent must be inferred from the facts. In our opening brief, we go into great detail on the types of facts that have been identified from which one can infer genocidal intent. We also demonstrate in our brief how the factual findings in the judgement match up with the suggested types of evidence you can use to prove genocidal intent. This argument is laid out in great detail in our brief, and I don't intend to repeat that argument this morning. Whether the target group is conceived as Bosnian Muslims, as the Trial Chamber did, or as non-Serbs, as we submit they should have, this evidence laid out in our brief demonstrates beyond a reasonable doubt that Dr. Stakic's intent was to destroy the targeted group in Prijedor. Now, there are two clues in the judgement, I think, as to reasons why the Trial Chamber may have failed to draw the obvious conclusion from its own findings of fact, and both of those are in paragraph 553 of the judgement. First, the Trial Chamber said that it was satisfied that the common goal of the members of the SDS in Prijedor, including Dr. Stakic, was to establish a Serbian municipality. However, they found that there was insufficient evidence of an intention to do so by destroying, in part, the Muslim group. The Trial Chamber believed the goal was, rather, to eliminate any perceived threats, especially by Muslims, to the overall plan and to force non-Serbs to leave the municipality of Prijedor. They said that security for the Serbs and protections of their rights seems to have been the paramount interest. By using the word "rather," the Trial Chamber thus found it inconsistent with genocidal intent that the ultimate goal was seen as security for the Serbs and protection of their rights. This, we submit, shows that the Trial Chamber confused motive with intent. The political, social, or economic reasons that underlie genocide are not inconsistent or incompatible with the intent to destroy a group. This Appeals Chamber cautioned against confusing intent with motives in the Jelisic appeal judgement. Whatever the ultimate political goal of the campaign was, we submit the means used to accomplish that goal in this case was by intended acts of genocide. A second clue while the Trial Chamber did not draw the obvious conclusions from its own findings of fact are also in paragraph 553 of the judgement. There the Trial Chamber said: Had the aim been to kill all Muslims, the structures were in place for this to be accomplished. The Trial Chamber observed that while approximately 23.000 people were registered as having passed through the Trnopolje camp, the total number of killings probably did not exceed 3.000. We submit that this reflects a fundamental misunderstanding by the Trial Chamber of the proper scope of genocidal intent. First, assuming that genocide only includes the intent to destroy a group by killing the members, there is nothing in the Statute that requires all members of the group be killed. Indeed, the Statute specifically recognises that the intent must be to destroy in whole or in part a national, racial, or religious group as such. We're also cautioned that there is no genocidal result that is required to prove genocide. In this case, to look at the number of victims and say that because not all victims were killed ignores the fact that we don't know what might have happened had events developed differently on the ground, had, for example, the Omarska camp not come to the attention of the Western authorities and the victims had been released. So that is the second problem with focussing on the number of victims. And third, the Statute specifically includes -- I'm sorry. Third, the Trial Chamber's decision implicitly assumes that the only way a group can be destroyed is by killing its individual members. The Trial Chamber equated destruction of the group to killing its members. I'd like to summarise the argument I want to present here, and then I'm going to expand a bit on these points. Our basic argument is: It is the group, as such, that is protected by Article 4 of the Statute, not the lives of the individual members. A group is more than the individuals that compose it. A group can be destroyed in whole or in part by first killing individual members of the group, particularly those of some prominence in the group, and then by obliterating the characteristics of the group so that it can never reconstitute itself as a group. We will also say that the goal of this genocide was to destroy non-Serbs as a presence in Prijedor municipality. In paragraphs 51, 327, and 703 and 706 of the judgement, it's noted that the Serb population increased from 42 per cent in 1991 to 96 per cent in 1993. The Trial Chamber concluded in paragraph 706 of the judgement that the common goal to create a Serb municipality in Prijedor had, in fact, been achieved. Had the proper legal test been applied to the evidence, the Trial Chamber would have concluded that not only did Dr. Stakic have the intent to destroy the target group in Prijedor, but that the intended destruction had largely been achieved. I'd like to expand a bit on each of these points. First, it is the group as such which is protected by Article 4, and not the individual alone. As the recent Blagojevic and Jokic trial judgement recognised, a group is comprised of its individuals, but also its history, its traditions, its relationships between its members, its relationships with other groups and its relationships with the land. I think Judge Shahabuddeen expressed the same idea in his separate opinion in Krstic, saying that a group is constituted by characteristics, often intangible, binding together a collection of people as a social unit. Although it's often stressed that genocide requires a physical or biological destruction, it is important to note that this destruction is of the group and not of the individuals in the group. This was recognised in paragraph 25 of the Krstic appeal judgement. And recently in the Blagojevic and Jokic trial judgement, the Trial Chamber observed that the physical or biological destruction of a group is not necessarily the death of the group members. Again, as Judge Shahabuddeen recognised in his separate opinion in Krstic, if the characteristics of a group have been destroyed in pursuance of the intent with which a listed act of physical or biological nature was done, it is not convincing to say that the destruction, though effectively obliterating the group, is not genocide because the obliteration was not physical or biological. The conclusion of the Commission of Experts, I submit, reaches the right conclusion on what it means to destroy a group. In paragraph 94 of their final report, they said: "If a group has its leadership exterminated and at the same time, or in the wake of that, has relatively large numbers of the members of the group killed or subjected to other Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. heinous acts, for example, deported on a large scale or forced to flee, the cluster of violations ought to be considered in its entirety in order to interpret the provisions of the convention in a spirit consistent with its purpose." With these principles in mind, let us look one more time at the findings of the Trial Chamber and determine whether any reasonable trier of fact could have concluded, as it did, that Dr. Stakic did not have the intent to destroy the Bosnian Muslim community, indeed, the entire non-Serb community in Prijedor. Even before the takeover in Prijedor, the press began publishing vicious propaganda against non-Serbs, paragraph 52. After the takeover, and as a result of the changes, tension and fear increased significantly among the non-Serb populations, paragraph 85. In paragraph 107, after the takeover, the propaganda campaign continued, this time focussing on prominent non-Serbs. The Trial Chamber found this was aimed at discrediting and undermining the credibility of the leaders of this community. Non-Serbs were ordered to surrender their weapons in an attempt to render them defenceless, paragraph 122. Non-Serbs were dismissed from their jobs, leaving them with no means of earning a living in the community, paragraph 125. And non-Serbs were ordered to mark their homes with a white flag. All of this occurred before most of the criminal activity that's alleged in this case even took place. Hearing this list, one is reminded of Lemkin's description of how a genocide typically progresses. According to Lemkin, genocide typically starts with the destruction of the national pattern of the oppressed group. This does not necessarily involve immediate extermination. More typically, it entails a series of coordinated acts designed and intended to slowly suffocate a group. Typically, these were directed against a collectivity's cultural institutions, language, religion, and physical integrity. What happened next in Prijedor shows even more clearly the intent of Dr. Stakic and others to destroy this group as a presence in Prijedor. Paragraph 129, attacks were directed at unarmed villages. In paragraph 154, the aims of these attacks in which some people were criminally murdered was to cleanse the villages of their non-Serb population. Can there be a clearer example of genocidal acts committed with the intent to destroy the group in those villages? Camps with brutal and deadly conditions were established in Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje. Killings were often directed at the leaders of the community. As we noted in paragraph 343 of our Appeal Brief, of 63 leaders and prominent individuals cited in the Prosecution's final trial brief as targeted, the Trial Chamber concluded beyond a reasonable doubt that most of them had in fact been killed. It's in paragraph 204 of the final trial brief and in the section of the judgement, section 6. The residual community was thus left without its leadership and the intent was to impair its ability to reconstitute itself as a group. Places of religious worship, Catholic and Muslim, were destroyed. Muslim homes were destroyed. Ultimately most of those not killed or who did not die from serious bodily or mental harm done to them or the conditions of life put on them were deported out of the area. Can there be any doubt that the aim of this programme was to ensure that the targeted group never reappeared in Prijedor municipality, that it be completely destroyed? I would now like to just briefly turn to the second ground of appeal, because it's an additional legal question that's related to this. In paragraph 557 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber concluded that the dolus specialis had not been proved in relation to "deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part." The Trial Chamber recalled in this context that deporting a group or part of a group is insufficient if it is not accompanied by methods seeking the physical destruction of the group. Its our submission that the Trial Chamber erred by considering only the act of deportation and by not considering other categories of evidence regarding conditions of life calculated to bring about the physical destruction of the group in whole or in part. In paragraph 517 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber correctly identified the types of conditions that could be conditions of life calculated to bring about the physical destruction of a group in whole or in part. However, when it actually applied this standard, the only fact it expressly considered was the act of deportation. In addition, it's our submission that the act of deportation was in this case accompanied by methods seeking the physical destruction of the group, and therefore as to the only evidence the Trial Chamber expressly considered, it got it wrong. In our appellant's brief, we list the facts proven at trial that should have been considered to be conditions of like deliberately inflicted on the group calculated to bring about its destruction. I'm not going to repeat those again. In paragraph 517 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber addresses, I think, the legal basis for the claim that methods of -- that these conditions of life can constitute methods of physical destruction. It's part of the genocide convention, of course, in paragraph -- in Article 4, section (2)(c) of our Statute, and it's also been discussed in cases before the Rwanda Tribunal, the Akayesu judgement, the Kayishema judgement, and others, and the Brdjanin judgement here before this Tribunal. I would like to conclude by looking at the events in Prijedor and the events recognised by this Appeals Chamber already as a genocide in Srebrenica. This Court in the Krstic case recognised that what happened in Srebrenica was properly characterised as a genocide. The events in Srebrenica occurred over a period of days. The events in Prijedor occurred over a period of months, yet genocide can be a slow process as well as a quick one. Let's look no further than paragraph 655 of the judgement, where the Trial Chamber said: "The Trial Chamber therefore considers that the killings committed in the municipality of Prijedor during the relevant period of 1992 were part of a campaign of annihilation of non-Serbs carried out by Serb police and military forces." Before I came down here this morning, I grabbed off of my desk my trusty dictionary that's been sitting there for 20 years, and looked up "annihilation." And its defined in two of its definitions: "to cause to cease to exist." And the very next definition: "To destroy a considerable part of," such as the army was annihilated. Can there be a clearer indication than this finding from the Trial Chamber that it erred when it found that there was no genocidal intent in this place? The events that took place in Prijedor was a genocide. Dr. Stakic was one of the most important leaders in this process. He was found guilty of extermination, murder, and persecution, and the persecution charge was founded on his discriminatory intent to commit acts of persecution, including murder, against the non-Serb population of Prijedor. He was a leader in the plan that the Trial Chamber concluded was designed to gain Serbian control over Prijedor at any cost. In this case, that cost included not only annihilation, but also genocide. I'm happy to answer any questions that you may have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. McKeon, you were talking about living conditions, and the subject was whether they were calculated to result in the destruction of the group in whole or in part. So to the question whether genocide was thereby accomplished. Now, would I be right in collecting from you that the Trial Chamber made no findings one way or the other on this point? If that is correct, then what remedy would you be asking for from this Appeals Chamber? Would you be asking the Appeals Chamber itself, independently, to make a finding, or would you be asking for some other remedy?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: I think the first remedy would be to look at the findings of fact that were actually made on related issues, and those are laid out in our brief on the conditions that were in the camps, and determine whether the Trial Chamber should have concluded from those findings of fact the way that we say it should have concluded. However, ultimately, if the Trial Chamber applied the wrong legal standard, then it is open to this Appeals Chamber, under the Blaskic authority, to independently determine the facts, applying the correct legal standard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. McKeon, you compared briefly the events in Prijedor to the events in Srebrenica, and you emphasised particularly the difference in the temporal element. Leaving aside the temporal element, it seems to me that the Appeals Chamber in the Krstic case dealt with the synergy between deliberate killing basically of all the males of a certain age and the expulsions. And I would be interested in knowing whether you feel that your argument measures with the guidelines developed in Krstic to how we approach, or at least how the majority in that case approached what constitutes genocide.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: I think that every individual case is going to be somewhat different and has to be examined on its own facts, and obviously the facts are not exactly the same here as they were in Srebrenica. However, you have many similarities. You have a large number of people killed and you have the remaining people driven from the municipality. You have targeted the leadership of the community, such that the community is left in exile, without its leaders. You have in Prijedor the destruction of the community ties that were left behind. You have in both cases the fact that the town was of a strategic importance in Srebrenica because it was in Western Bosnia, and Prijedor because it was in the north, in the corridor area, and therefore had an importance because of that. And in Prijedor, as the judgement indicates, you had a town that was known as an area where the ethnic groups enjoyed peaceful relations, and so therefore, targeting the ethnic groups could deliver a message to the remaining non-Serbs in the rest of Bosnia. So I think you have to look at each case individually and you have to look at the facts that are on this case as presented. Whether a given fact is not here that may have been in Srebrenica I don't think is determinative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCKEON
utterances.text: I'm actually finished. If there are no other questions, then I'd like to turn over the podium to my colleague, Mr. Tracol, to address the fourth ground of appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Tracol, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] President and Appeals Chamber, I shall now address the fourth ground of appeal relating to cumulative convictions. In 2003, the Prosecution appealed the cumulative convictions for persecutions and other crimes against humanity by relying on the same facts in the Martinovic and the Naletilic case and Stakic case. In the Kordic and Cerkez judgement in paragraph 1039 to 1044, the Appeals Chamber held that cumulative convictions for persecutions and the other three crimes against humanity, namely, murder and other inhumane acts and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. imprisonment is legitimate in that it relies on the same facts. Under Article 5 of the Statute, the Appeals Chamber still has to determine whether cumulative convictions for persecutions and other crimes against humanity, such as expulsion and torture, are legitimate. I shall make my submissions before the Appeals Chamber in two weeks' time in the Martinovic and Naletilic case regarding cumulative convictions for persecution and torture. In the Stakic judgement, the Trial Chamber committed an error in law in paragraphs 879, 880 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I'll stop you for a minute. Thank you very much. Judge Pocar is very learned technologically and resolved the problem in no time, together with the registrar. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRACOL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me resume. In the Stakic judgement, the Trial Chamber committed an error in law in paragraphs 879, 880, and 881 of the judgement by not convicting Milomir Stakic for the Counts 3, murder as a crime against humanity, and Count 7, deportation as a crime against humanity, of the indictment. The Trial Chamber claimed that in exercising paragraph 870 of the judgement, its discretionary powers, it can make a finding of guilt solely for the crime which specifically and in a comprehensive manner, clearly accounts for his criminal conduct. This position is contrary to the materially distinct element test set out by the Appeals Chamber in the Delalic judgement. Position of the Prosecution is as follows: The Trial Chamber committed an error when it applied the cumulative conviction test as it was interpreted by the Appeals Chamber in the relevant case-law. The findings of the Trial Chamber in paragraphs 879 to 883 of the judgement do not accord with those of the Appeals Chamber in paragraph 1040 to 1043 in the Kordic and Cerkez judgement as far as the test applies to persecutions and murder in the Kordic and Cerkez judgement, paragraph 1041. The Appeals Chamber concluded that persecutions contain elements materially distinct from murder, namely, that persecutions require that an act or omission which introduces a discriminative fact be proven and also that an act or omission was committed with the specific intent to discriminate Conversely, murder requires that proof of death be provided of one or several people, which is not the case for persecution. The Appeals Chamber concluded that cumulative convictions for persecutions and murder is legitimate in that it relies on the same facts in accordance with Article 5 of the Statute. The Appeals Chamber rightly concluded that persecutions and murder meet the test set out by the Appeals Chamber in the Delalic judgement inasmuch as those two crimes contain at least one materially distinct element which is lacking in the other. Persecutions and murder therefore constitute distinct crimes according to the international criminal law even if the criminal conduct remains the same. Persecutions can be committed without there being proof of murder, so long as the underlying acts deny and infringe upon a fundamental right. The proof of murder is therefore not required for persecutions. The Trial Chamber is right in entering a finding of guilt in the Cerkez and Kordic judgement, that cumulative convictions for persecution and murder is legitimate as it relies on the same facts pursuant to Article 5 of the Statute. How the test applies to cumulative convictions for persecutions and deportation. The Trial Chamber has not had the opportunity to adjudicate on the legitimacy of cumulative convictions for persecutions and deportation. In addition, there is, I believe, no ICTR case-law on this particular issue. As the Appeals Chamber concluded in the Kordic and Cerkez judgement, paragraph 1041 and 1043, persecution require proof of an act or omission which discriminates in fact and -- on the one hand, and proof that an act or omission was committed with a specific intent to discriminate, on the other hand, whereas deportation is sufficient to establish that a fundamental right has been denied or infringed upon. Deportation is not required to enter a conviction for persecution. Persecution, therefore, continual element that is materially distinct from deportations. In addition, deportation requires that proof of the intention to transfer the victim be proven. Deportation requires proof of an element that is materially distinct from persecutions. The Prosecution submits that, on the basis of the same reasoning, the grounds in the Kordic and Cerkez judgement logically leave the Appeals Chamber to conclude that cumulative convictions for persecutions and deportation is legitimate on the basis of the same facts under Article 5 of the Statute. In the Kordic and Cerkez judgement, the Appeals Chamber applied the same reasoning to persecution and other inhumane acts in paragraph 1042 and imprisonment in paragraph 1043. As regards persecution and other inhumane acts, the Appeals Chamber considered in the Kordic and Cerkez judgement, paragraph 1042, that the other inhumane acts require proof of the fact that the accused infer grave mental and physical suffering on the victims, which is not a requisite for persecutions. The Appeals Chamber thus concluded that a cumulative conviction for persecution and other inhumane acts is legitimate on the basis of the other facts under Article 5 of the Statute. As far as persecution and imprisonment is concerned, the Appeals Chamber considered in the judgement of Cerkez and Kordic, paragraph 1043, imprisonment require that deprival of liberty be opposed arbitrarily, which is not a requisite for persecution. The Appeals Chamber thus concluded that cumulative conviction for persecution and imprisonment is legitimate on the basis of the same facts under Article 5 of the Statute. In the Blagojevic and Jokic judgement, I here refer specifically to paragraphs 807 to 810 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber expressly referred to the findings in the Kordic and Cerkez judgement pertaining to cumulative convictions for persecution and murder, on the one hand, and persecutions and other inhumane acts, on the other hand. The Trial Chamber in Blagojevic and Jokic applied the same findings as in the Kordic and Cerkez judgement. Neither party appealed these findings of the Trial Chamber. For the case in point, in the test is correctly applied, the Appeals Chamber must enter a conviction for persecution, on the one hand, in accordance with Article 5(h) of the Statute, and for deportation, on the other hand, in accordance with Article 5(f) of the Statute as crimes legally distinct. The Prosecution submits that this finding complies with Kordic and Cerkez in the interests of justice and would not in any way lead to an unwarranted prejudice for Mr. Stakic. If the Trial Chamber had correctly applied the conviction test, it would have convicted Mr. Stakic for persecution, Count 6 of the indictment, on the one hand, for murder, and Count 3 of the indictment, for which it entered a finding of guilt, paragraph 632 and 872, and lastly, for deportation, Count 7 of the indictment, for which it has also entered a finding of guilt, paragraph 712 and 872. I have concluded my submission and would be prepared to answer any questions from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tracol. I will ask my colleagues whether ... no, we -- I gather that the Judges will not ask you questions now. So we will now conclude our hearings for today and reconvene at 9.00 a.m. tomorrow morning. We will rise now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 5th day of October, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.28 p.m.,
